Abstract
Hafnium (Hf) oxide-based ferroelectric materials have emerged as a transformative platform for next-generation
non-volatile memory and advanced computing technologies. This review comprehensively examines the development, chal-
lenges, and applications of HfO2 ferroelectrics, emphasizing their CMOS compatibility, scalability, and robust polarization at
nanoscale dimensions. Breakthroughs in doping strategies, stress engineering, and VO control have stabilized the metastable
orthorhombic phase, enabling high-performance devices such as ferroelectric RAM (FeRAM), ferroelectric ﬁeld-eﬀect transis-
tors (FeFETs), and ferroelectric tunnel junctions (FTJs). These devices oﬀer ultrafast switching, low power consumption, and
multi-level storage, driving innovations in neuromorphic computing, in-memory processing, and cryogenic systems; nonethe-
less, they face ongoing challenges in reliability, such as fatigue and imprint eﬀects, and scalability at sub-5 nm technology
nodes. Emerging frontiers, such as wurtzite-structured nitrides (e.g., AlScN) and antiferroelectric ZrO2-based systems, have
garnered signiﬁcant attention due to their exceptionally high remanent polarization and promising potential for enhanced
endurance, respectively. Further addressing the reliability issues of these emerging ferroelectric materials and the challenges
associated with large-scale integration processes through interdisciplinary eﬀorts will unlock the full potential of ferroelec-
tric technologies, positioning them as pivotal enablers of post-Moore computing architectures and sustainable AI-driven
applications.

Introduction
The exponential growth of data-intensive technologies, ranging from artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) and
machine learning (ML) to the Internet of Things (IoT) and edge computing, has exposed the limitations
of conventional computing and memory architectures [1–3]. Traditional von Neumann systems, which
separate memory and processing units, struggle with energy ineﬃciency and latency bottlenecks, while
mainstream non-volatile memory (NVM) technologies, such as Flash, face fundamental trade-oﬀs among
speed, endurance, scalability, and power consumption [4, 5]. In this landscape, ferroelectric materials
have garnered signiﬁcant attention in recent years due to their unique polarization switching properties,
which enable a range of applications in memory and logic devices [6–8]. Among these materials, hafnium
(Hf) oxide-based (HfO2-based) ferroelectrics have emerged as a breakthrough due to their compatibility
with modern complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) technology, scalability to sub-10 nm di-
mensions, and robustness under extreme operating conditions, which bridging the gap between emerging
computing paradigms and scalable, CMOS-compatible hardware solutions [9,10].
Ferroelectric materials, which exhibit switchable spontaneous polarization under an external electric
ﬁeld, have long been envisioned as ideal candidates for NVM due to their inherently fast switching speeds,
low operating voltages, and robust reliability.
However, traditional perovskite-based ferroelectrics (e.g., Pb(Zr,Ti)O3) suﬀer from critical drawbacks,
including poor compatibility with CMOS processes, thickness-dependent ferroelectricity, and environ-
mental concerns related to lead content [11]. These challenges have catalyzed a paradigm shift toward
ﬂuorite-structured oxides, particularly HfO2, following the groundbreaking discovery of ferroelectricity
in silicon-doped HfO2 thin ﬁlms in 2011 [12]. The unique attributes of HfO2-based ferroelectrics, in-
cluding CMOS compatibility, scalability to sub-10 nm thicknesses, and robust polarization at nanoscale
dimensions, position them as a disruptive enabler for advanced memory and logic devices. The rapid
development of ferroelectric hafnium has opened new possibilities in both logic and memory devices,
including ferroelectric ﬁeld-eﬀect transistors (FeFETs), ferroelectric capacitors, and ferroelectric tunnel
junctions (FTJs). These devices enable various advanced functionalities, such as nonvolatile memory,
in-memory computing, and neuromorphic processing, which are critical for AI acceleration, low-power
computing, and high-speed data storage. In particular, FeFETs and ferroelectric random-access mem-
ory (FeRAM) based on HfO2 exhibit signiﬁcant advantages in terms of switching speed, endurance, and
retention, positioning them as strong candidates for beyond-von Neumann architectures [13].
Despite these promising developments, HfO2-based ferroelectric materials and devices continue to face
several critical challenges. The fundamental mechanisms underlying ferroelectricity in doped and undoped
HfO2, including the stabilization of the metastable orthorhombic phase, require further investigation [14].
Additionally, process variations, wake-up eﬀects, fatigue, and retention issues are not only related to the
ferroelectric phase structure of the HfO2-based material but also to the complex defect behaviors, such
as oxygen vacancies (VO), within the material, which pose signiﬁcant hurdles for large-scale industrial
adoption [15–17].
These factors contribute to reliability issues in related devices, which include not
only the most commonly reported problems of device endurance and retention, but also more complex
challenges, such as the read-after-write issue in FeFETs, program/read disturb in ferroelectric device
arrays, and the increased design complexity of both arrays and peripheral circuits arising from these
issues [18,19].
In addition to the extensively studied HfO2-based ferroelectric technologies, several other ferroelectric-
related approaches have garnered signiﬁcant attention from researchers due to their unique performance
advantages and potential applications.
These include zirconium oxide (ZrO2)-based antiferroelectric
(AFE) materials and devices, wurtzite-structured ferroelectric materials, and domain-wall-based fer-
roelectric devices.
Antiferroelectricity can be observed in Zr-rich HfZrOx (HZO) or pure ZrO2 thin
ﬁlms [20,21]. Studies have shown that by employing electrode or interface engineering, a non-symmetrical
built-in potential can be introduced into the material [21, 22]. This manipulation can shift double hys-
teresis loops of antiferroelectric in one direction, allowing the utilization of a single loop to realize NVM
functionality in metal-ZrO2 (or HZO)-metal device structures. Experimental results have demonstrated
that ZrO2-based antiferroelectric devices oﬀer higher polarization switching endurance and operate at
lower voltages compared to their HfO2-based ferroelectric counterparts. Another promising category is
the wurtzite-structured ferroelectric materials, with scandium (Sc)-doped AlN (AlScN) being the most
representative [23]. AlScN exhibits distinctive features not observed in HfO2-based ferroelectric ﬁlms,
including a high remnant polarization (Pr) typically exceeding 100 µC/cm2, an exceptionally high Curie

Basic mechanisms of HfO2-based ferroelectrics
HfO2-based ferroelectric materials have attracted signiﬁcant attention in recent research and have shown
potential in various applications, such as non-volatile memories, sensors, and actuators. This section aims
to elucidate the basic mechanism of the emergence of HfO2-based ferroelectricity, including the eﬀects of
stress, doping, and so on [24].
2.1
Phase structure and ferroelectricity
The HfO2 materials with ﬂuorite structure possess several phase structures. The non-polar monoclinic
(m-) phase is thermodynamically stable with a space point group of P21/c at room temperature and
pressure. In high temperatures, hafnium oxide tends to appear in cubic (Fm¯3m) phase structures with a
high symmetry [25]. During the cooling process, the cubic phase undergoes a transition to the tetragonal
(t-) phase (P42/nmc).
By suppressing the growth of the m-phase through a selective rapid thermal
annealing process, the polar orthorhombic (Pca21) phase can be obtained [12]. The orthorhombic (o-)
phase is a common ferroelectric phase in HfO2-based ferroelectric materials and has a speciﬁc crystal
structure and symmetry. The displacement of polar oxygen atoms leads to spontaneous polarization. In
the unit cell, three-coordinated polar oxygen atoms are separated by four-coordinated nonpolar oxygen
atoms. Thus, each electric dipole in ferroelectric Hf oxide can be switched independently regardless of
size eﬀects [26]. Due to the bistability of o-phase, m-phase, and t-phase is often present in HfO2 thin
ﬁlms [27]. Factors such as stress, doping, and external ﬁeld stimulation may induce phase transition
processes, which can alter the ferroelectric behavior.
The VO concentration and the surface energy
inﬂuenced by the electrochemical state can change the polarization intensity, internal bias ﬁeld, and
other electrical properties by aﬀecting the polar orthorhombic phase [28,29].
Moreover, a rhombohedral (R3m) polar phase (r-phase) with higher energy can be obtained by design-
ing speciﬁc constraints [30]. Wang et al. [31] discovered a CMOS compatible rhombohedral ferroelectric
Hf(Zr)1+xO2 material rich in Hf(Zr). Excessive Hf(Zr) atoms embedded in the lattice of the thin ﬁlm
can stabilize the ferroelectric rhombohedral crystal structure (Figures 1(a) and (b)). Density functional
theory (DFT) calculations reveal that the formation energy of the r-phase is lower than those of the
o-phase and m-phase in Hf(Zr)-rich Hf(Zr)O2 ﬁlms when the ratio of Hf(Zr) to O is larger than 1.079:2,
which is more conducive to the formation of the r-phase (Figure 1(d)). Hf (Zr) interstitial atoms enhance
the ferroelectricity of the thin ﬁlm and reduce its ferroelectric polarization switching barrier (Figures 1(e)
and (f)), resulting in an ultra-low coercive electric ﬁeld (EC) of 0.65 MV/cm and a small saturation
polarization ﬁeld (1.25 MV/cm) (Figure 1(c)). Most importantly, the device demonstrates a lifetime
exceeding 1012-cycles at saturation polarization. This material discovery may help to realize low-cost
and long-life memory chips.

This phase structure change is closely
related to the lattice distortion, atomic displacement, and energy change induced by stress.
The clamping eﬀect from the top and bottom electrodes can eﬀectively enhance ferroelectricity. For
example, for the preparation of HfO2 thin ﬁlms by atomic layer deposition, introducing top electrode
coverage before rapid thermal annealing results in a signiﬁcant increase in polarization compared to the
case without top electrode [32]. This may be due to the tensile stress introduced by the combined action
of the top and bottom electrodes during the annealing process. Tensile strain can modify the lattice
structure of HfO2-based materials, increasing the lattice spacing. This aﬀects the electronic structure
and polarization behavior, potentially leading to an increase in ferroelectric polarization and a change
in the Curie temperature. In addition, diﬀerent electrode types can eﬀectively modulate the associated
ferroelectric behavior by changing the interfacial state and reducing the VO concentration [33,34].
Moreover, the stress from the substrate also aﬀects the ferroelectric properties of HfO2-based ferro-
electric materials. During the growth of single-crystal HfO2-based ferroelectric ﬁlms, as the substrate
lattice parameter increases, the phase structure of HfO2 gradually changes from a monoclinic phase to
the coexistence of m- and o-phases, and then to the predominance of o-phase [25, 35]. This indicates
that in contrast to the tensile strain, compressive strain causes the lattice to contract and increases the
electrostatic interaction between ions, restricting the movement of ions and thus being unfavorable for
the formation and maintenance of the o-phase.
2.3
Inﬂuence of doping on HfO2-based ferroelectric materials
Doping elements aﬀect the ferroelectric properties of HfO2-based materials by altering the crystal struc-
ture, chemical bonding, charge distribution, and energy state of the material. For example, some doping
elements may change the type of chemical bonds between atoms, making them more conducive to the
generation of polarization. The ionic radius, valence state, and dopant concentration of the doping el-
ements also aﬀect their occupancy in the lattice and their interaction with surrounding atoms, thereby
inﬂuencing the phase structure and ferroelectric properties of the material.

3
Impact of VO on ferroelectric properties
The ferroelectric properties of HfO2-based materials can be signiﬁcantly inﬂuenced by the presence of
VO, which plays a fundamental role in determining the material’s polarization characteristics [48–58].
The concentration, distribution, and migration of these vacancies dictate not only the stability of the
ferroelectric phase but also the device’s endurance and fatigue behavior [17, 59–61]. Understanding the
impact of VO is crucial for optimizing these materials for practical applications, as their presence can
both enhance and degrade the material’s properties.
The stability of o-phase, which is essential for
ferroelectricity, is mainly governed by the local conﬁguration of VO. However, the ability to control
the concentration and distribution of VO provides a valuable means of manipulating the ferroelectric
properties. Research has demonstrated that VO inﬂuences several key characteristics of ferroelectricity,
such as Pr and EC, and plays a central role in phenomena like the wake-up eﬀect and fatigue degradation.
3.1
Role of VO in stabilizing ferroelectricity and reliability
VO in HfO2 is integral to the formation and stabilization of the ferroelectric orthorhombic phase, which
is necessary for ferroelectricity to manifest. VO creates local distortions in the crystal lattice that lower
the energy barrier for the transformation from the tetragonal to the orthorhombic phase, facilitating
the stabilization of this polar phase. The presence of VO thus acts as a “trigger” for the ferroelectric
phase, enabling the material to maintain a non-zero Pr. However, the concentration of VO is a critical
factor: too few vacancies can result in an insuﬃciently stabilized orthorhombic phase, leading to weak
or non-existent ferroelectric properties. On the other hand, excessively high concentrations of VO can
cause phase instability, leading to defects, such as the formation of non-ferroelectric monoclinic phases,
and degradation in ferroelectric properties.
Experimental studies and DFT calculations have shown
a strong relationship between VO concentration and Pr in HfO2 [17, 59]. With the VO concentration

this point, further increases in VO concentration led to a decrease in Pr, as the lattice becomes destabilized
and defects begin to accumulate. This has been conﬁrmed by various studies, which demonstrate that

of HfO2.
Chen et al. [59] investigated the possible mechanisms of wake-up and fatigue by developing a phase-
ﬁeld polarization switching model for ferroelectric HfO2-based thin ﬁlms, considering VO. The “wake-up”
eﬀect is an important phenomenon in HfO2-based ferroelectrics, which occurs during electric ﬁeld cycling.
When a fresh HfO2 thin ﬁlm is initially polarized, it often exhibits a “pinched” P-V hysteresis loop, where
the Pr is suppressed. It has been demonstrated that this behavior is due to an uneven distribution of VO
within the ﬁlm, often resulting in localized regions with poor ferroelectric characteristics. However, upon
applying an electric ﬁeld for several cycles, these VO redistribute spontaneously, leading to a more uniform
concentration of vacancies throughout the material. As a result, the ferroelectric response is “woken up”,
and the P-V hysteresis loop becomes more conventional, with an increase in Pr. While the wake-up eﬀect
can enhance the ferroelectric properties of HfO2, excessive electric ﬁeld cycling eventually leads to fatigue.
Fatigue is characterized by a gradual decrease in Pr, typically caused by the continuous generation and
migration of VO during cycling. High concentrations of VO accumulate over time, disrupting the stability
of the orthorhombic phase, which ultimately leads to phase transitions to the non-ferroelectric m-phase.
Fatigue behavior is a critical challenge for the long-term reliability of ferroelectric devices, and managing
VO concentration is key to mitigating this issue. Research has shown that the fatigue eﬀect is closely
tied to the migration of VO [59, 61]. VO is not uniformly distributed throughout the ﬁlm; it tends to
accumulate at grain boundaries and interfaces with electrodes, where they are more likely to migrate into
the bulk of the material. This migration accelerates the degradation of ferroelectric properties. Strategies
such as doping, interface engineering, and the use of superlattices can help mitigate the migration of VO
and slow down the fatigue process.
Besides wake-up and fatigue, a phenomenon observed in certain doped HfO2-based ﬁlms is the recovery
of ferroelectric properties after fatigue. This “recovery eﬀect” occurs after a period of high electric ﬁeld
cycling or annealing. Understanding and controlling this process is key to developing durable and reliable
ferroelectric devices, particularly in applications that involve repeated cycling or high-ﬁeld stress. Chen
et al. [60] have experimentally and theoretically conﬁrmed that the ferroelectric fatigue and recovery in
doped-HfO2 under an external electric ﬁeld (Eext) is dominated by the redistribution of VO, rather than
the charge detrapping eﬀects. The fatigue under low Eext is mainly due to the non-uniform distribution
of VO caused by migration in the in-plane direction during the polarization switching, while the recover
under high Eext can be attributed to the VO uniformly redistribution (Figure 2). As the VO concentration
becomes more uniform, the stability of the ferroelectric phase increases (Figure 2 [60]). This recovery
mechanism opens up possibilities for designing self-healing ferroelectric devices, where the material can
recover its ferroelectric properties after prolonged use, potentially extending the lifespan of the device.
3.2
Enhancing endurance through VO engineering
To improve the endurance of HfO2-based ferroelectrics, researchers have focused on engineering the
migration and concentration of VO. One promising strategy is the use of HfO2-ZrO2 superlattices (SLs).
Recent studies have highlighted the superior endurance and fatigue recovery characteristics of HfO2-ZrO2
SL ferroelectric capacitors compared to conventional HZO counterparts [62–64].
Peng et al. [62] reported the fabrication and comprehensive characterization of metal-ferroelectric-
metal (MFM) capacitors using tantum nitride (TaN) electrodes and two types of ferroelectric ﬁlms—
conventional HZO solid solution and an SL structure composed of alternating HfO2 (12 ˚A) and ZrO2
(12 ˚A) layers, both with a total thickness of 10 nm. As shown in Figure 3(a), high-resolution transmission
electron microscopy (HRTEM), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and grazing-incidence X-ray
diﬀraction (GIXRD) analyses were used to compare the microstructural and crystallographic features of
the HZO and HfO2-ZrO2 SL stacks. In particular, the high-angle annular dark-ﬁeld (HAADF)-TEM
image highlights the well-deﬁned periodicity of the superlattice, with the lattice mismatch between HfO2
and ZrO2 introducing compressive strain, while the annular bright-ﬁeld (ABF)-TEM image conﬁrms the
presence of the orthorhombic Pca21 ferroelectric phase in the SL structure. GIXRD patterns further
reveal a pronounced peak at ∼30.5◦(orthorhombic (111)), indicative of strong ferroelectricity in both
ﬁlm types.

of the ﬁlm. This is crucial for maintaining the material’s ferroelectric properties over time. Moreover,
the increase in migration energy barriers also reduces the rate of VO generation, which further improves
the material’s resistance to fatigue. By optimizing the thickness of the individual layers and the overall
structure of the superlattice, researchers can ﬁne-tune the properties of these materials to achieve the
desired balance between high polarization and long-term stability.
In addition to SL, doping strategies that increase the formation energy of VO can also improve the
endurance of HfO2-based devices. Elements like lanthanum (La), Si, and Zr can be doped into HfO2 to
modify the energy landscape, making it more diﬃcult for VO to form and migrate. This can result in a
more stable ferroelectric phase and reduced fatigue.

the ferroelectric layer and an interfacial layer (IL) of titanium oxynitride (TiOxNy) [17]. This allows for
precise modulation of the ferroelectric properties by controlling the VO concentration and distribution
within the ﬁlm.
In an MFM structure, the interfacial layer acts as a reservoir for VO, enabling its
reversible injection into and extraction from the HfO2 ﬁlm under electric ﬁeld stress. This mechanism
of reversible VO migration provides a unique opportunity for tuning the Pr of HfO2-based ﬁlms. By
adjusting the duration and amplitude of the electric pre-stress pulse, diﬀerent ferroelectric states can be
achieved and reversed on demand, oﬀering a new way to control the material’s properties.

Phases and structural evolution in HfO2-based ferroelectric ﬁlms
4.1
Origin of ferroelectric orthorhombic phase formation
The doped HfO2 ferroelectric ﬁlms, prepared through atomic layer deposition (ALD), initially mainly
exhibit a disordered amorphous structure. Upon undergoing rapid thermal annealing (RTA) with the
clamped electrodes, the ﬁlms crystallize into randomly oriented polycrystalline structures with grain sizes
on the order of tens of nanometers. The resulting crystal phases include monoclinic (m: P21/c), tetragonal
(t: P42/nmc), non-ferroelectric orthorhombic (oI: Pbca or oII: Pnma), and ferroelectric orthorhombic
(oIII: Pca21) structures. Notably, the ferroelectric o-Pca21 phase is considered to be responsible for the
robust ferroelectricity in HfO2-based ﬁlms. To identify potential ferroelectric phases in HfO2, Sang et
al., using the position-averaged convergent beam electron diﬀraction (PACBED) method, experimentally
demonstrated the existence of a non-centrosymmetric o-phase that can support spontaneous polarization
in Gd:HfO2 ﬁlms [65]. Luo et al. [66] and Zheng et al. [67] utilized Cs-TEM combined with the STEM-ABF

4.2
Structural evolution and its implications for wake-up and fatigue
The structural evolution of HfO2-based ferroelectric thin ﬁlms under electric ﬁelds plays a pivotal role in
the wake-up and fatigue eﬀects, which signiﬁcantly inﬂuence the performance of ferroelectric memories.
The wake-up eﬀect refers to the gradual increase in Pr after an initial period of electrical cycling. In
contrast, fatigue is characterized by a progressive degradation in Pr with increasing cycling, ultimately
leading to a reduction in device performance and durability. These phenomena not only aﬀect the device
reading window but also impose limitations on the long-term reliability of ferroelectric memory devices,
closely associated with their structural evolution.
One signiﬁcant mechanism for the wake-up eﬀect is the t-to-o phase transition in HfO2-based ﬁlms.
Kim et al. [73] demonstrated that as electrical cycling increases, there is a decrease in the dielectric
constant of the ﬁlm, indicating a phase transition from the high-dielectric constant t-phase to the low-
dielectric constant o-phase. Grimley et al. [74] observed phase changes at the interface region of the
ﬁlms using ex-situ TEM. Zheng et al. [75] applied an in-situ bias to the HZO ferroelectric capacitor,
inducing a phase transition from the t-phase to the ferroelectric o-phase (Figure 5(a)), highlighting that
such t-to-o phase transitions undoubtedly contribute to ferroelectricity enhancement. It is worth noting
that when the t-to-o transition is not fully completed, a t-/o-coherent structure often forms within a
single grain, facilitating the o-to-t reversible transition under the inﬂuence of a temperature ﬁeld [74,76].
Additionally, 90◦ferroelastic domain transition signiﬁcantly contributes to the wake-up eﬀect. Shimizu et

5.2
Performance and reliability in cryogenic
As the CMOS technology enters the post-Moore era, aggressive scaling is no longer a practical way
for performance and density improvement. Novel computing architectures like in-memory computing
and emerging devices with ultralow power consumption, negative capacitance ﬁeld eﬀect transistors
(NCFET), and tunneling FET (TFET), are considered and intensively explored for their potential use
as an alternative to the current Si CMOS technology. Low temperature high performance computing
(LT-HPC, 77 K) and cryogenic quantum computing (QC, 4 K) are such potential alternative solutions
for higher computing capacity and lower power consumption. For any computing chips working at low
temperature (LT), memory units are necessary to implement the energy-eﬃcient LT system together with
the logic units. Among the several modules in the superconducting QC system, the lack of a scalable and
compatible 4 K memory is a key challenge and limits the superconducting electronics to primary-stage
commercialization.
So far, the LT memory can be categorized into three major groups: cryogenic non-superconducting
memories, superconducting memories, and hybrid memories. More detailed information on these memo-
ries implemented with the traditional CMOS technology can be found in [97]. For novel memory technolo-
gies, like the HfO2-based FeFETs and FeRAMs, the properties of HfO2-based ferroelectric at cryogenic
temperature (CT) are getting signiﬁcant attention with the rise of quantum-computing systems, space
electronics, and superconducting processors [98–100]. As compared with LT memories implemented with
resistive RAM (RRAM), magnetoresistive RAM (MRAM), or phase change RAM (PCRAM), few stud-
ies have reported the performance of LT ferroelectric memories [95, 101–110]. While the properties of
archetypal perovskite-based ferroelectrics have been studied in great detail over the last seven decades all
the way from above 1400 K down to the mK range [95,101–103], there exist only a few similar studies on
the ﬂuorite type oxide ferroelectrics (i.e., HfO2 based ones) at a temperature range of 4–1200 K [104–110].

Recent progress and applications on FeRAM
6.1
Endurance and performance optimization of FeRAM
Since the discovery of hafnia-based ferroelectric materials, a variety of memory devices have been
developed, leveraging their unique properties for emerging non-volatile memory applications. Among
them, hafnia-based memory devices primarily include FeFETs, FeRAM, and FTJs. Notably, FeRAM in-
herits the structural simplicity of dynamic random access memory (DRAM) and stands out as a promising
candidate for practical implementation due to its mature fabrication processes [116–120]. The typical
structure of the FeRAM bitcell is 1T1C type shown in Figure 9(a), comprising one ferroelectric capaci-
tor and one series-connected select transistor. In this setup, the word-line (WL) controls bitcell access
through the transistor gate, while the bit-line (BL) and plate-line (PL) facilitate driving the bitcell during
operation. FeRAM utilizes Pr in a ferroelectric capacitor for data storage, with polarization switching
enabling data readout. During the readout process, the ferroelectric capacitor in the selected bitcell is po-
larized to its saturation state, and the charge diﬀerence between stored data “1” and “0” is distinguished
by the bitline voltage diﬀerence during readout (Figure 9(a)).
Despite its advantages in low-power consumption and high-speed operation, FeRAM faces signiﬁcant
challenges related to reliability and scaling. Due to the multi-grain nature and intrinsic high switching
electric ﬁeld of HfO2-based ferroelectric materials, HfO2-based ferroelectric capacitors typically endure
only ∼1010 cycles before experiencing hard breakdown under saturated polarization switching [121–123],
falling short of the endurance requirements of conventional DRAMs. To address this limitation, sub-
loop operation strategies supplemented with re-wake-up pulses have been discovered and widely adopted,
extending FeRAM endurance to ∼1014 cycles under reduced operating voltages [124–126].
However,
operating at lower voltages introduces additional complications.
Apart from the reduced switchable
polarization, the switching dynamics of ferroelectric capacitors may cause unexpected memory access
issues [127], which require further investigation and optimization tailored to the unique characteristics
of FeRAM. For example, dynamic-induced memory window degradation has been observed, where the
dynamic nature of ferroelectric switching impacts the readout process, causing severe MW reduction
(Figures 9(b) and (c)) [128]. To address these challenges, researchers have proposed asymmetric operation

6.2

Scaling FeRAM to higher densities is becoming a primary focus of ongoing research. For traditional

Recent progress and applications on FeFET
7.1
High endurance Si channel FeFETs
HfO2-based FeFET is one of the most promising candidates for future non-volatile memory, due to its
ultra-low power consumption, high speed, and good scalability. However, FeFET applications remain
constrained by limited endurance, primarily attributed to charge trapping and trap generation during
cycling [139]. In the commonly used metal-ferroelectric-interlayer-semiconductor (MFIS) structure, the
ferroelectric material and interlayer (IL) signiﬁcantly inﬂuence charge trapping dynamics, directly im-
pacting endurance.
Thus, the choice of gate stack materials is critical for achieving high-endurance
FeFETs. For HfO2-based ferroelectric layers, reducing the EC and spontaneous polarization density (Ps)
can mitigate the electric ﬁeld within the interlayer (EIL). Concurrently, interlayers with high dielectric
constant (κ) and thermal stability are essential to minimize EIL and avoid low-κ oxide generation at the
Si interface. Additionally, the ferroelectric-interlayer interface must exhibit low trap density (Nit) and
strong process compatibility, as summarized in Figure 12(a).
Following this guideline, a co-optimization of ferroelectric and interlayer materials has been demon-
strated using Hf0.95Al0.05O2 (HAO) and Al2O3 as ferroelectric and interlayer, respectively (Figure 12(b))
[140]. Compared to the common HZO, HAO exhibits lower Ps and EC, while Al2O3 oﬀers superior κ
and thermal stability over SiO2. These materials also maintain excellent thermal compatibility and high
interface quality, extending the endurance of HAO+Al2O3 FeFETs to >5×109 cycles, which is 3 orders
of magnitude higher than the baseline HZO FeFET (Figure 12(c)). For the analysis of co-optimization,
a novel double quasi-static CV (DQSCV) measurement conﬁrmed the reduced trapped electron and
hole densities (Ne and Nh), indicating lower Nit at the ferroelectric-interlayer interface, as shown in
Figure 12(d).
FeFETs also support multi-level cell (MLC) storage through partial polarization behavior, enhancing
storage density. However, MLC FeFETs face severe device-to-device variation and endurance issues [141].
To address these challenges, a reliable MLC FeFET was developed via novel co-optimization of ferroelec-
tric gate stacks and writing pulses (Figure 12(e)) [142]. For device uniformity, inserting a thin Al2O3
layer between the two HZO layers decreases the grain size to suppress the device-to-device variation.
Moreover, employing writing pulses with larger amplitude and shorter width further suppresses the ran-
dom ferroelectric domain switching. The average standard deviation (σavg) for the threshold voltage
(Vth) distribution after co-optimization achieves a 36% reduction compared to the standard HZO FeFET,

FeFET-based CIM
NVM-based computing in memory (nvCIM) architectures generally perform MAC operations in a voltage-
domain analog way. Relatively high VDD to accommodate the dynamic range of amplitude signals, as
well as complex data-conversion analog blocks with large power, is inevitable for voltage-mode nvCIM.
To address the problem of voltage scalability, a novel FeFET-based time-domain (TD) nvCIM with both
MAC operation and activation function has been implemented (Figures 15(a)–(c)) [172]. By utilizing
the cumulative propagation delay of a cascaded inverter chain to realize the accumulation of MAC, the
FeFET-based TD nvCIM can signiﬁcantly improve the energy eﬃciency, along with high compatibility
with digital circuits. Beneﬁting from the three-terminal transistor structure, the fabricated FeFET can
function as both a nonvolatile element for weight storage and a controllable switch for neural network
input modulation simultaneously, thereby realizing local multiplication of MAC in the proposed ferroelec-
tric delay unit with only 2T-1FeFET. The novel dual-edge operation is also demonstrated for TD MAC,
enabling further energy eﬃciency improvement. Furthermore, by utilizing the physics of time-dependent
gradual polarization switching, FeFET as the activation function for TD nvCIM with additional memory
trace behavior for deep reinforcement learning is experimentally demonstrated with only a single tran-
sistor [173]. The FeFET-based TD nvCIM provides a promising area- and energy-eﬃcient mixed-signal
neural network for edge AI.
Moreover, for nvCIM, the weight-parameter data stored in NVM can be easily retrieved by directly
accessing the NVMs, rendering potential security vulnerabilities of IP stealing and adversarial attacks.

7.5
FeFET-based neuromorphic computing
Brain-inspired neuromorphic computing architectures have triggered a lot of interest due to event-driven
features and high energy eﬃciency. The basic computing elements of neuromorphic systems are still
mostly CMOS-implemented and suﬀer from a high hardware cost issue, especially when expanding ad-
vanced functions.
Recently, a novel concept of leaky-FeFET (L-FeFET), a HfO2-based FeFET with
accelerated polarization degradation, has been introduced for neuromorphic computing (Figures 16(a)
and (b)) [176,177]. This innovation was designed to mimic biological neuron behaviors with a minimal
hardware cost, enabling the development of a novel capacitor-less neuron of basic leaky integrate-and-ﬁre
function with only one transistor and one resistor. The unique characteristics of L-FeFET are further
explored for advanced neuronal functions. A novel spiking neuron capable of both excitatory and in-
hibitory connections for unsupervised learning, utilizing only three transistors, which was made possible
by leveraging the physics of bi-directional ferroelectric polarization accumulation (Figures 16(c)–(e)) [176].
Furthermore, through device-circuit co-design, the adaptively-stochastic function is incorporated into the
neuron to support simulated annealing algorithms, which capitalizes on the intrinsic random dynamics
of ferroelectric domain nucleation, enabling an all-FeFET spiking neural network for optimization with
signiﬁcantly improved area-eﬃciency (Figures 16(f)–(i)) [178,179]. The FeFETs have provided a highly
integrated neuron solution for neuromorphic computing systems, opening new possibilities for eﬃcient
and innovative computing paradigms.

8.1
Advantages and challenges of HfO2-based FTJ
FTJs are a new type of tunneling eﬀect device based on ferroelectric materials. The basic structure of
an FTJ consists of two metal electrodes with a nanometer-thick ferroelectric material layer in between,
typically with a thickness of 5–10 nm, which ensures that quantum tunneling can occur eﬀectively [180].
When an external electric ﬁeld is applied, the polarization direction of the ferroelectric layer changes,
resulting in a change in its resistance state. This phenomenon is referred to as the tunneling electroresis-
tance (TER) eﬀect [181]. In FTJs, when the polarization direction of the ferroelectric material reverses,
the magnitude of the tunneling current changes signiﬁcantly, leading to a variation in the device’s re-
sistance. This resistance change enables data storage and retrieval. Even when the power is turned oﬀ,
the polarization state of the ferroelectric material remains stable, allowing the FTJ to provide persistent
data storage, thus exhibiting non-volatile memory characteristics.

lower operating voltage. By adjusting the doping and thickness of HfO2 ﬁlms, the ferroelectric properties
can be eﬀectively tuned, leading to the further optimization of FTJ device performance. Research has
shown that the ON/OFF ratio of HfO2-based FTJ devices can reach 102–106, and the write voltage can
be reduced to around 3 V, signiﬁcantly enhancing the application potential of FTJs [188].

and SRAM. To address this issue, researchers are exploring new materials and structural designs to
break through the speed bottleneck and achieve sub-nanosecond switching speeds. Second, although
a thin ferroelectric layer helps achieve high ON current for tunneling, it limits the TER ratio due to
reduced polarization [190]. Moreover, as the number of cycles increases, ferroelectric polarization may
generate interface traps, which can aﬀect current switching performance and further limit the application
of HfO2-based FTJ devices [191].
The applications of FTJs are not limited to traditional memory ﬁelds, their potential in neuromorphic
computing is also promising. Neuromorphic computing simulates the signal transmission between neurons
in the brain, where information is transmitted through “synapses”, similar to weight updates in artiﬁcial
neural networks. As memristive synapse devices, FTJs have the potential to mimic biological synapse
functions [192]. By adjusting the resistance state of FTJ devices, it is possible to replicate synaptic
transmission between neurons, providing a new approach for implementing neural networks.
Despite the existing challenges, with continuous optimization of silicon-compatible materials and the
development of neuromorphic computing applications, FTJ devices are expected to become a key com-
ponent in the future of non-volatile memory and computing. Further in-depth research into their ma-
terial properties, device structures, and application potential will help drive breakthroughs in the next-
generation storage and computing technologies.
8.2
Performance and reliability enhancement of Hf-based FTJ
Carrier modulation through the use of semiconductor electrodes can signiﬁcantly enhance the interface
shielding length diﬀerence, thereby increasing the switching ratio to more than 100%. However, semicon-
ductor electrodes are prone to forming parasitic layers at the interface and inducing depolarization ﬁelds,
which may weaken device stability. To address this issue, the researchers optimized the ferroelectric phase
stability of HfZrO (HZO) by symmetric energy band design [193], combining the ZrO2 seed layer with
the Al2O3 barrier layer to further improve the switching ratio while suppressing the depolarization ﬁeld,
which provides a new way of thinking about the high-reliability ferroelectric tunnel junction (FTJ).
The durability of ferroelectric devices is limited by the internal bias ﬁeld induced by oxygen vacancy
migration, leading to the hindered electric domain ﬂip-ﬂop. La/Al co-doped HfO2 ﬁlm technology is
proposed to enhance the residual polarization to 30 µC/cm2 by suppressing oxygen vacancy diﬀusion,
and to achieve a fatigue life of 107 cycles at a high temperature of 300◦C [194]. In addition, NH3 plasma
treatment of the TiN/HZO interface reduces the defect density and suppresses the imprinting eﬀect [195],
while the HfO2-ZrO2 superlattice structure suppresses the defect diﬀusion through the periodic potential
barriers, which improves the fatigue recovery capability by three times and signiﬁcantly extends the
device lifetime [64].
Multiferroic tunneling junction (MFTJ) based on magneto-electric coupling eﬀect employs LSMO/
BaTiO3/LSMO heterojunctions to achieve polymorphic storage [196].
Hafnium-based FTJs, on the
other hand, achieve 10-state storage in a single device through precise regulation of electrical pulse
amplitude/timing. For high-density storage requirements, the self-rectifying FTJ cross-array technology
reduces cell area and power consumption to achieve increased storage density.
Hafnium-based FTJs, on the other hand, reduce the ﬂip-ﬂop time to 78 ns by adjusting the oxygen
vacancy concentration through La/Ta co-doping [197]. In addition, the combination of ultra-small elec-
trodes and layered interface structure achieves a switching speed of 780 ps at 2 V, which is close to the
limit of electronic devices [198].

The intriguing FeFET characteristics, including 3-terminal structure, good CMOS compatibility, and the
high on/oﬀratio, make FeFET emerge as a promising candidate in CIM designs. In analog CIMs, as
shown in Figure 19(a), multiple rows are activated simultaneously and the outputs from the cells, either
current or voltage, are accumulated and converted to digital signals via analog-to-digital converters

transistor-like structure of FeFETs can achieve AND/NAND array structure to improve the memory
density, and the FeFET high ON/OFF ratio facilitates more reliable computation.
The ﬁrst FeFET-based CIM design for matrix-vector multiplication (MVM) was proposed in 2017
using the cell circuit shown in Figure 19(a) [9]. Afterward, various studies have proposed to leverage the
FeFET unique characteristics for improved CIM performance. Ref. [215] optimized the resistor in 1T1R
cell to achieve ultra-high 13700TOPS/W energy eﬃciency. Refs. [214,216] utilized the high compatibility

for improved density, respectively. A recent work in [217] further exploits the 3D FeFET NAND array
to enlarge the memory capacity, achieving support for large-scale graph neural networks, as shown in

reliability while taking advantage of the FeFET characteristics to enhance performance.

FeFETs for security applications in IoT scenarios
In the era of the IoT, the extensive deployment of IoT devices such as intelligent sensors and edge AI across
areas like home automation, smart cities, and healthcare has driven a massive demand for cloud-edge
data interactions. Meanwhile, these edge devices connect to the cloud, which stores sensitive user keys,
behavioral data, and commercial secrets, making them vulnerable to attacks and posing potential risks of
data leakage [228]. Security risks arise throughout the data collection, transmission, and processing stages,
as shown in Figure 20(a). Identity attacks involve impersonation, where attackers disguise themselves as
legitimate users to illegally access cloud-stored data. Asset attacks include direct data theft from edge
memory through methods such as reverse engineering and brute force, targeting sensitive information in
sensors, communication devices, and pre-trained weights in edge AI. Leakage attacks, on the other hand,
extract data from the cloud through malware or by directly eavesdropping on messages from cloud-edge
communication channels [229].
Thus, comprehensive data protection for IoT devices is needed, even under constraints of hardware
costs such as area and power. FeFET enables low-cost in-memory computing modules using compact
1T AND-type arrays, suitable for various edge security applications.
Its ultra-low write power and
higher on/oﬀratio compared to RRAM reduce power consumption [6]. Moreover, the FeFET’s three-

The ferroelectric layer’s grain and domain spatial distribution, along with domain switching dynamics,
contribute to signiﬁcant device-to-device and cycle-to-cycle stochasticity, providing a reliable entropy
source for hardware security primitives. Overall, FeFET is highly suitable for secure applications in IoT
scenarios.
To address identity attacks, physically unclonable functions (PUFs) leverage unpredictable physical

ZrO2-based antiferroelectric for memory applications
ZrO2-based AFE has attracted extensive attention for its higher switching speed and endurance in com-
parison to its ferroelectric counterparts, showcasing its great potential in next-generation memory tech-
nologies [12,247]. Additionally, a low operating electric ﬁeld can be achieved by utilizing half of the double

access memory. It is reported that boosted antiferroelectricity without compromising the endurance is
achieved by applying ozone (O3) treatment to the bottom electrode (BE) of AFE capacitors [20]. Besides,

Three kinds of fatigue mechanisms are revealed [251]. (1) Extrinsic fatigue occurs due to VO charge
trapping at the TiN/HZO interface. The trapped VO creates an imprint electric ﬁeld that alters the
energy barrier for polarization switching, leading to asymmetric hysteresis loops and performance degra-
dation. (2) Intrinsic fatigue includes two mechanisms. (i) AFE-to-FE phase transition: Localized VO
facilitates a phase transition from the AFE Pbca o-phase to the ferroelectric Pca21 o-phase, diminishing
AFE properties. (ii) VO localization: Tetra-coordinated VO in the lattice stabilizes conﬁgurations that
increase switching barriers, reducing polarization switching eﬃciency. This work provides a comprehen-
sive understanding of how VO inﬂuences AFE performance and identiﬁes strategies for improving device
endurance.

For memory applications, a key challenge for AFE devices is how to alleviate the volatile eﬀect of AFE

no fabrication process adjustment and could be more ﬂexible.

11.1
Growth and ferroelectricity of wurtzite ferroelectrics
The development of wurtzite-phase III-nitride ferroelectrics, such as AlScN and GaScN, has garnered sig-
niﬁcant attention due to their unique ferroelectric properties. Density functional theory studies by Zhang
et al. [269] revealed that these alloys exhibit stable wurtzite phases up to Sc compositions of approxi-
mately 0.56 for AlScN and 0.66 for GaScN. Beyond these limits, rock-salt phases become energetically
favorable. Despite the challenges in achieving pure wurtzite phases, this structure is critical for realizing
the ferroelectric potential of III-nitride semiconductors [212, 213]. A range of deposition methods has
been explored for Sc-III-N alloys, including reactive magnetron sputtering [270–272], molecular beam
epitaxy (MBE) [273–276], metal-organic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD) [277–280], hydride vapor
phase epitaxy (HVPE) [281–283], and PLD. Among these, epitaxial techniques like MBE and MOCVD
oﬀer superior control over compositional uniformity, crystallinity, and impurity incorporation.
Although theoretical predictions for ferroelectricity in Sc-III-nitride materials were proposed two
decades ago, experimental validation remained elusive until 2019. The challenge was to lower the switch-
ing energy barrier while maintaining the dielectric breakdown strength of the material. This milestone was
ﬁnally achieved by Fichtner et al. [23], who demonstrated ferroelectric switching in sputtered polycrys-
talline AlScN ﬁlms with Sc concentrations of up to 40%. In 2021, Wolﬀet al. [284] provided further insight
through detailed TEM studies, conﬁrming switchable polarization in AlScN at the atomic scale. These
foundational studies have since spurred intensive research into the ferroelectric properties of sputtered
AlScN, with numerous investigations exploring its potential and mechanisms in greater depth [285–293].
In 2021, Wang et al. [59] achieved a signiﬁcant breakthrough by demonstrating fully epitaxial, single-
crystalline ferroelectric AlScN ﬁlms on n-GaN substrates. These epitaxial ﬁlms exhibited coercive ﬁelds
ranging from 3 to 6 MV/cm and remnant polarization values between 120–150 µC/cm2. Additionally, they
demonstrated exceptional retention time exceeding 105 s and endurance over 107 cycles [294–296]. Most
recently, ferroelectric polarization switching has also been achieved in MOCVD-grown AlScN ﬁlms [297],
indicating the scaling production of wurtzite nitride ferroelectrics in the future. Except for AlScN, fer-
roelectric polarization switching has also been achieved in wurtzite GaScN [298–300], YalN [301], and
BalN [302,303] in the past years.
It is important to note that, in addition to the Sc doping concentration, strain eﬀects, particularly in-
plane tensile strain, also inﬂuence the switching energy barrier, i.e., the EC, in AlScN ﬁlms, and contribute
to the enhancement of ferroelectric performance [290]. Li et al. [304] investigated the impact of residual
stress in Al0.8Sc0.2N ﬁlms with diﬀerent electrode materials. The use of platinum (Pt) electrodes improved

11.4
Fatigue mechanisms in ferroelectric AlScN ﬁlms: the role of oxygen inﬁltration
To enable high-performance non-volatile ferroelectric memory technologies, ensuring robust polarization
switching endurance in ferroelectric materials is essential. Despite their promising properties, wurtzite-
structured ferroelectric memories face substantial limitations due to endurance degradation. The mi-
croscopic origins of such fatigue remain elusive, as most prior investigations have relied primarily on
macroscopic electrical measurements, oﬀering limited physical insight into the degradation pathways.
In a landmark study, Wang et al. [321] delivered the ﬁrst direct microstructural evidence clarifying
fatigue mechanisms in AlScN thin ﬁlms. Their work identiﬁed oxygen inﬁltration as a critical contributor
to endurance loss. Using TEM and EDS, the authors traced the dynamic migration of oxygen atoms in
Al0.65Sc0.35N ﬁlms that underwent repeated electrical cycling. Wang et al. [321] utilized a typical AlScN
ferroelectric capacitor fabrication process that involves depositing a ∼450 nm Al0.65Sc0.35N layer between
Pt bottom and Ti/Au top electrodes. The Al0.65Sc0.35N ﬁlm was sputtered at ∼400◦C using an Al-Sc
alloy target in a nitrogen-argon plasma to promote crystallinity. Top electrodes are patterned as 90 µm ×
90 µm squares via shadow masking. This structure was commonly used for evaluating device endurance
and switching performance.

ingress along grain boundaries, leading to structural degradation within the ﬁlm. Remarkably, by elim-

capacitors to achieve an endurance of 4.6 × 107 cycles while sustaining a high Pr of 114.6 µC/cm2. These

Ferroelectric domain walls are two-dimensional topological interfaces between two domains in diﬀerent
orientations, with thicknesses approaching the unit cell level of the 180◦walls. The walls exhibit electrical

moving interfaces. This allows real-time adjustment of their positions, densities, and orientations [342–

domain walls oﬀer a wide range of functional electric and magnetic properties, and serve as excellent two-

12.1
Domain wall memristors
In 2014, the concept of a ferroelectric domain-wall memory was patented [348], where non-destructive
readout of domain wall currents and device structures was opened four years later [349]. (Figures 35(a)
and (b)). This approach involves the fabrication of paired nanoelectrodes in various nanogaps on BFO
using electron beam lithography.
It is found that the coercive voltage gradually decreases with the
narrowing of the nanogap. The domain switching time is as short as 100 ns with the endurance cycling
number over 107 [349]. In the same period, Sharma et al. [350] also reported a solid-state non-volatile
domain wall data storage device using asymmetric coplanar metal contacts on BiFeO3 (BFO) (110) thin
ﬁlms (Figures 35(c) and (d)) in 2007. Besides the coplanar memory devices, other constructions are using
conductive domain walls in center-type topological quadrant domains, epitaxially grown within BFO
nano-islands. However, it is challenging to grow BFO at high temperatures (∼650◦C) for the fabrication
of domain wall memories in the CMOS platform. The additional hurdle toward commercialization is
low readout currents (pA to nA level) that are generally required on the order of 10 µA to drive a fast
memory circuit with read time less than 1 ns.
The advancement of “Smart-cut” technology, which produces high-quality, large-area lithium niobate
(LN) ﬁlms in nanometer-to-micron thicknesses chemically bonded to silicon wafers (LiNbO3-on-insulator,
LNOI), oﬀers new routes for the development of ferroelectric domain wall memories. The domain wall
memory was fabricated on the surface. Encoded data are read through the creation and annihilation
of persistent and transient domain walls within each mesa-like cell [351], where a slightly tilted 180◦-
like domain wall and a “dead layer” at the interface act as a conducting channel and a homogeneous
embedded selector, respectively (Figures 35(e) and (f)). These mesa-structured memory cells that can
be shrunk below 20 nm [352] and be operated at low voltages by extending the side electrodes to the
mesa surface [353], exhibit an exceptionally high on/oﬀratio of over 106 with endurance exceeding a
billion of cycles [351], enabling the integration of a high-density crossbar memory [354]. To improve
the device performance, many studies have been devoted to the studies of the imprint eﬀect [355], large
domain wall currents [356], temperature stability [357,358], downscaling capability [359], nanofabrication
conditions [360,361], and embedded electrode materials on polarization retention and fatigue [361]. For
the multilevel storage, advancements in domain wall devices are also reﬂected in their ﬂexible and tunable
multi-resistance states. Domain walls exhibit unique electronic properties in the number that can be ﬁnely
controlled by the applied voltages and/or a series of pulses, allowing for adjusting multiple resistance levels
within a single device (on current ∝wall number). This adaptability is crucial for developing advanced
memory technologies and paves the way for implementing memristor functionalities. Experiments have
shown that doping, defects, temperature, strain, and electric ﬁelds can all tune the electronic conductance
of domain walls, enabling the development of multifunctional or multilevel memristors [362].
The domain walls can be classiﬁed into neutral walls and charged head-to-tail and tail-to-tail walls. The
two polarizations terminating at the domain walls determine the localized charge state (Figure 35(g)).
Charged walls can have the uncompensated domain boundary charge, leading to the formation of a two-
dimensional electron gas in high mobility and the observation of resonant electron transport in tunnel
junctions [362–364]. By controlling the conﬁguration of the walls in tilted angles and thus their charge
states, a three-state domain wall memory has been realized (Figure 35(h)) [365–367]. After bending or
controlling the wall subsurface topology, the multilevel information storage is realized through tunable
conducting states [367–369]. Alternatively, the number of domain walls can be tuned by applying voltages
in the readout of domain wall currents, leading to multilevel storage (Figure 35(i)). A four-state domain
wall memory was developed on LNOI. Each state is operated stably at a speciﬁc low voltage to tune
up/down the number of domain walls (Figures 35(i) and (j)) [370]. Besides the wall number, the total

Unique electronic properties emerge when domain walls interact with diﬀerent electrode materials,
resulting in a diode-like behavior at the interface. For instance, in ErMnO3, neutral domain walls exhibit
diode properties at the electrode-domain junction, facilitating AC-DC conversion and an atomic-level
half-wave rectiﬁer based on ferroelectric domain walls [376]. Using scanning microwave impedance mi-
croscopy, the GHz-frequency AC response of domain walls in Lu0.6Sc0.4FeO3 single crystals was detected.
The response is controlled by vibrational dynamics, with AC conductivity about 104 times higher than
DC conductivity [377]. Meier et al. [378] observed an asymmetric current-voltage dependence through the
conductive atomic force microscope (CAFM) tip detection of charged domain walls, where the Schottky
barrier at the tip-sample contact is essential to the rectiﬁcation behavior. Therefore, both the interfacial
“dead” layer in LiNbO3 and voltage-modulated domain wall geometry contribute to the diode-like prop-
erties. A half-wave rectiﬁer device was successfully demonstrated using these phenomena [356,374,379].
The atomic-level domain-wall diodes whose lateral dimensions are deﬁned by the smallest contact area
potentially surpass standard metal-semiconductor junctions and enable domain-speciﬁc rectiﬁcation in
ferroelectrics [347,380].

In summary, unlike artiﬁcially created oxide interfaces (heterogeneous interfaces), domain walls as
homogeneous interfaces display diﬀerent degeneracy and symmetry from the host material, resulting in
new physical properties not found in the surrounding domains. The use of domain walls as conductive
channels provides low power consumption and good reliability in fast operations better than RRAM.
Further, domain-wall memories are moving into lab-to-fab technology validation, with possible architec-
tures of 1T1R, Crossbar, and 3D stacking. As the fabrication of 8 to 12-inch LiNbO3 single-crystal ﬁlms
appears mature in the market, the prospect of commercial LNOI domain-wall memories is growing. It is
also worth noting that using the intrinsic properties of ferroelectric domain walls to control the current
and mimic the behavior of electronic components, rather than controlling conductivity by injecting and
erasing the walls, oﬀers additional opportunities for developing domain wall nanoelectronics.

Conclusion
The rapid evolution of HfO2-based ferroelectric materials and devices has positioned them as a cornerstone
for next-generation NVM and advanced computing paradigms. Over the past decade, breakthroughs in
material engineering, phase stabilization, and device architecture have unlocked unprecedented oppor-
tunities for integrating ferroelectric functionalities into CMOS-compatible platforms. This review has
systematically explored the development, challenges, and transformative potential of HfO2-based ferro-
electrics, highlighting their critical role in bridging the gap between emerging computing architectures and
scalable hardware solutions. The discovery of ferroelectricity in doped HfO2 thin ﬁlms marked a paradigm
shift, enabling robust polarization in ﬂuorite-structured oxides at nanoscale dimensions. Key advances in
doping, stress engineering, and VO control have elucidated the stabilization of the metastable orthorhom-
bic phase. However, challenges persist in fully understanding phase-transition dynamics, defect-mediated
polarization switching, and the interplay between interfacial strain and reliability. Innovations such as
superlattices and hybrid doping strategies have demonstrated enhanced endurance by suppressing VO
migration. However, achieving uniform phase distribution and mitigating wake-up/fatigue eﬀects remain
critical for industrial adoption.
HfO2-based devices, including FeRAM, FeFETs, and FTJs, have shown remarkable progress. FeFETs,
with their ultra-low power consumption and compatibility with 3D integration, are pivotal for embedded
NVM and neuromorphic computing. FeRAM architectures, leveraging sub-loop operations and asymmet-
ric pulse schemes, achieve endurance exceeding 1014 cycles, yet dynamic polarization degradation during

density and energy eﬃciency challenges, though variability and endurance limitations demand further
optimization. FTJs oﬀer high-speed, low-power memory and synaptic functionalities, though scaling to
sub-nanosecond switching speeds and improving TER ratios requires novel interfacial engineering.
Beyond traditional memory, HfO2-based ferroelectrics are driving innovations in neuromorphic com-
puting, in-memory logic, and cryogenic applications. The analog tunability of polarization states enables
synaptic plasticity and energy-eﬃcient vector-matrix multiplication, critical for AI accelerators. At cryo-
genic temperatures, HfO2-based devices exhibit enhanced retention and endurance, aligning with the
demands of quantum and low-temperature computing systems. DTCO strategies, such as 3D stacking
and hybrid memory-logic platforms, are essential to overcoming scalability and reliability bottlenecks
while maximizing density and performance.

The future of HfO2-based ferroelectrics lies in multidisciplinary collaboration across materials science,
device physics, and systems engineering. Advances in in-situ characterization, machine learning-driven
material discovery, and heterostructure design will accelerate the transition from lab-scale breakthroughs
to commercial adoption. As the semiconductor industry ventures into the post-Moore era, HfO2-based
technologies stand poised to redeﬁne the boundaries of computing eﬃciency, adaptability, and sustain-
ability, enabling transformative applications in AI, edge computing, and beyond. By addressing existing
challenges through innovation and co-design, these materials will cement their role as enablers of the next
technological revolution.

Abstract: Hafnium (Hf) oxide-based ferroelectric materials have emerged as a transformative platform for next-generation non-volatile memory and advanced computing technologies. This review comprehensively examines the development, chal- lenges, and applications of HfO2 ferroelectrics, emphasizing their CMOS compatibility, scalability, and robust polarization at nanoscale dimensions. Breakthroughs in doping strategies, stress engineering, and VO control have stabilized the metastable orthorhombic phase, enabling high-performance devices such as ferroelectric RAM (FeRAM), ferroelectric ﬁeld-eﬀect transis- tors (FeFETs), and ferroelectric tunnel junctions (FTJs). These devices oﬀer ultrafast switching, low power consumption, and multi-level storage, driving innovations in neuromorphic computing, in-memory processing, and cryogenic systems; nonethe- less, they face ongoing challenges in reliability, such as fatigue and imprint eﬀects, and scalability at sub-5 nm technology nodes. Emerging frontiers, such as wurtzite-structured nitrides (e.g., AlScN) and antiferroelectric ZrO2-based systems, have garnered signiﬁcant attention due to their exceptionally high remanent polarization and promising potential for enhanced endurance, respectively. Further addressing the reliability issues of these emerging ferroelectric materials and the challenges associated with large-scale integration processes through interdisciplinary eﬀorts will unlock the full potential of ferroelec- tric technologies, positioning them as pivotal enablers of post-Moore computing architectures and sustainable AI-driven applications.
